source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With the right answer used as a stop signal (oracle), self-correction looks strong. Without it, accuracy falls.
numbers: GPT-3.5 oracle vs standard: GSM8K 84.3 vs 75.9; CommonSenseQA 89.7 vs 75.8; HotpotQA 29.0 vs 26.0. GPT-4 oracle vs standard: GSM8K 97.5 vs 95.5; CSQA 85.5 vs 82.0; HotpotQA 59.0 vs 49.0.
quote: the improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: Oracle labels are not available in real tasks. Earlier gains in Reflexion and RCI used them.
agent_relevance: G2 stays valid: a revision needs real failing output, not the model's opinion. Any gain measured with a hidden answer is not evidence for self-critique.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no outside feedback) lowers accuracy over rounds. Models flip correct answers to wrong ones.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8 -> 38.1 (round 1) -> 41.8 (round 2). GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Models: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2-70b; temperature 1 for GPT. Later work (c20) says temperature and prompt wording drove part of the drop.
agent_relevance: Do not add a generic review-your-answer pass. It can cost accuracy. Keep revision gated by located evidence (S5).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Multi-agent debate is mostly self-consistency in disguise. At equal number of responses, plain majority vote beats debate.
numbers: GSM8K, gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, full test set: standard 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2; debate (3 agents, 2 rounds, 9 responses) about 83.0 (table order garbled in PDF extraction, so debate cells are approximate).
quote: The observed improvement is evidently not attributed to "self-correction", but rather to "self-consistency".
limits: Du et al. used 100 GSM8K items; this replication used all of them.
agent_relevance: Spend a compute budget on sampling and voting before critique rounds.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Reported Self-Refine gains in constrained generation come partly from a weak first prompt. A better first prompt beats the loop, and the loop then hurts.
numbers: CommonGen-Hard concept coverage: Madaan baseline 44.0 -> self-correct 67.0 (as cited); the authors' improved plain prompt scores above the self-corrected number and self-correction lowers it again (about 81.8 -> 75.1; table cells partly garbled).
limits: Cell alignment in the extracted table is uncertain; direction is clear from the text.
agent_relevance: When testing a revise step, compare against the best single-pass prompt, not a sloppy one.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs (TACL)
finding: Survey of self-correction papers up to May 2024. No prior work shows success with feedback from a prompted LLM in general tasks; it works where reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning can teach it.
numbers: Prior wins flagged as unfair: use of oracle information, weak initial prompts, unequal compute. Bottleneck named as feedback generation.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey cutoff May 2024; later reasoning models only briefly covered. Exceptions are tasks with decomposable responses.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: let code or tools generate the feedback; let the model write the fix.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (BIG-Bench Mistake)
finding: Models are poor at finding the first wrong step in a chain of thought, but good at fixing it once told where it is.
numbers: Dataset: 2,186 CoT traces from PaLM 2 on 5 BIG-Bench tasks, step-level human labels. GPT-4 best at 52.87 overall mistake-finding accuracy (direct step-level prompting). Task cells: logical deduction GPT-4 40.67; multistep arithmetic GPT-4 44.00; GPT-3.5-Turbo 2.00 on logical deduction.
quote: LLMs clearly struggle with mistake finding, even in the most simple and unambiguous cases.
limits: Humans agree highly on labels. Traces are from one model family.
agent_relevance: Locating the error is the hard part. Code should locate it (G2), the model should fix it.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) BIG-Bench Mistake, backtracking experiment
finding: Given the true mistake step, regeneration helps far more than it harms. A random step gives much smaller gains.
numbers: Absolute change in accuracy, true location (correct-originals / incorrect-originals): word sorting -0.00 / +18.04; tracking shuffled objects -11.11 / +23.53; multistep arithmetic -6.67 / +43.92; Dyck -11.43 / +36.86. Random location: losses -6.67 to -15.91, gains +5.16 to +21.57.
limits: Uses oracle location from the dataset; false alarms break already-correct answers.
agent_relevance: A false alarm is expensive (-7 to -11 points on correct traces). A located-error trigger must have high precision.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) BIG-Bench Mistake, how accurate must the finder be
finding: Backtracking with a noisy error-locator still helps once the locator is about 60-70% accurate. A small trained classifier beat a large prompted model on some held-out tasks.
numbers: Net gain exceeds net loss near 60-70% classifier accuracy; losses plateau near 65%. Small PaLM 2 Otter vs 3-shot PaLM 2 Unicorn on held-out tasks: word sorting 22.33 vs 11.67; Dyck 33.57 vs 10.98; logical deduction 6.00 vs 6.67.
limits: Classifier trained out-of-domain; the authors say it does not reach the needed threshold overall.
agent_relevance: A cheap trained or rule-based checker may beat asking the big model to self-audit.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: On graph coloring, GPT-4 as its own verifier hallucinates errors and rarely accepts a correct answer. A sound external verifier helps, but the content of its feedback barely matters.
numbers: 100 instances: no backprompting 16% correct. Self-critique loop: 1 of 100 correct. Of 40 instances where the generator at some point produced a correct coloring, the LLM verifier missed it in all 40; in 39 it invented same-colored adjacent pairs. Only 4 of 100 runs were stopped by the LLM verifier, none correct. Sound verifier: nearly 40%, same for pass/fail, first-error or all-errors feedback.
quote: The correctness and content of the criticisms ... seems largely irrelevant
limits: One domain, one model, 100 instances, 15 iterations. Independent higher-temperature samples reach similar totals, so gains look like extra tries.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against LLM-as-stop-judge. The stop test should be code. Feedback detail may matter less than extra attempts.

source: Stechly et al. (2023) graph coloring, local fix rates
finding: Models obey error reports, true or false. They fix whatever they are told is wrong.
numbers: Share of mentioned edges changed: first-error 94% (1004/1066); full list any 98% (1077/1102); full list all 84%; evil backprompt naming a random correct edge as wrong: 94% (1017/1083) changed.
limits: Local fix does not mean overall correctness; performance stayed flat.
agent_relevance: Models are credulous to critique. A false error report from a bad critic gets repaired into new damage. Verify the report before acting.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: In Blocksworld planning an LLM verifier gives false positives, so LLM+LLM loops are worse than LLM + sound validator.
numbers: 100 instances: generator alone 40%; LLM+LLM backprompting 55% (3.48 iterations); LLM+VAL (sound validator) 88% (4.18). Verifier accuracy 61/100; accepted 54/55 valid plans; passed 7/45 invalid plans (15.55% false positives). 50-instance subset: binary feedback 74%, first error 86%, all errors 86%.
limits: Single domain, GPT-4. Table cell labels read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: A sound verifier is worth +48 points here; a model verifier +15. Same lesson as G2.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: In code, self-repair under equal sampling budget often gives small or no gain. The bottleneck is the model's explanation of why code failed. A better explainer unlocks the gain.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each is 1.05x pass@20; 2 initial plus 10 repairs each is 0.97x pass@22. Repair success with GPT-4's own feedback 33.30% vs human feedback 52.60% (1.58x); by difficulty 42.64 vs 62.21 (intro), 19.33 vs 45.67 (interview), 3.67 vs 14.67 (competition).
limits: Failing tests were given, so the finder was already supplied. Human study is small.
agent_relevance: Even with the failing test shown, diagnosis is the weak link; prefer diverse first drafts over many repair rounds.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Self-feedback loops help on style and preference tasks but not on math, because the model cannot spot the error.
numbers: Claim: about 20% absolute average gain. Examples: sentiment reversal GPT-3.5 8.8 -> 30.4; dialogue 36.4 -> 63.6 (first column) but 23.9 -> 27.5 and 27.3 -> 36.0 in the other two; math reasoning 64.1 -> 64.1 (no gain).
quote: a consistent-looking reasoning chain can deceive LLMs
limits: Table columns partly garbled in extraction. Huang et al. (c04) show part of the gain came from weak baseline prompts.
agent_relevance: Self-feedback suits subjective polish, not correctness.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion stores a written lesson after a failed trial and tries again with it. Gains rely on a pass/fail signal from the environment.
numbers: ALFWorld +22% absolute over baselines in 12 steps; HotPotQA +20%; HumanEval 91% pass@1 vs GPT-4 80%. On HotPotQA CoT with ground-truth context, 39% of questions stayed wrong; Reflexion lifted accuracy by 14%.
limits: Depends on binary success signals, unit tests or exact match; Huang (c01) flags this as oracle use.
agent_relevance: This is the design behind G2: reflection helps when the failure signal is real. Lessons carry across trials, not inside one.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Tool feedback (search, code run) gives real corrections. The same loop without the tool gives much less.
numbers: One QA table (first column, ChatGPT): CoT 44.2, CRITIC 50.0, CRITIC without tool 42.0, ReAct 47.6, ReAct+CRITIC 51.4.
limits: Column dataset labels not recoverable from text extraction; direction (tool > no tool) holds across rows I saw.
agent_relevance: Tools turn critique from opinion into evidence.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Multi-turn RL on self-made traces gives the first clearly positive intrinsic self-correction. Prompting and plain SFT did not.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash, MATH500: base 52.6 -> 41.4 on turn 2 (-11.2); Self-Refine 52.8 -> 51.8 (-1.0); STaR 53.6 -> 54.0 (+0.4); Pair-SFT 52.4 -> 54.2 (+1.8); SCoRe 60.0 -> 64.4 (+4.4). Right-to-wrong flips 15.8% base vs 1.4% SCoRe; wrong-to-right 9.5% base vs 14.5% SCoRe. HumanEval gain 9.1%.
limits: Training, not a scaffold; needs weights.
agent_relevance: Untouched models flip correct answers. A scaffold must stop that (keep best-so-far, G2).

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the Self-Correction Blind Spot (COLM 2026)
finding: The same error is fixed when shown as the user's mistake but not when shown as the model's own. The model can correct; it does not.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Closed: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-math (BIG-Bench Mistake logic and tracking): 62.8%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces cuts it 76.0%.
quote: models correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones
limits: Controlled injection; on-policy errors checked on two other sources.
agent_relevance: Human parallel: people miss their own slips. Present the model's earlier answer as someone else's draft for review.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench, Wait marker
finding: Appending the word Wait after the model's own mistake brings back correction with no training.
numbers: Wait cuts the blind spot by 89.3% on average. A role direction in representation space gates correction; Wait acts through a nearly independent route. Over 98% of SFT data lacks correction sequences.
limits: Open non-reasoning models; reasoning models already emit such markers.
agent_relevance: Cheap cue at S5: reframe own output as external and cue a pause.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing a reasoning model to keep thinking by appending Wait when it tries to stop makes it re-check and raises accuracy.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24 50% -> 57% with budget forcing; trained on 1,000 samples; beats o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24.
limits: Needs a reasoning model; gains flatten at long budgets.
agent_relevance: A Wait cue is a cheap slip-catch (an attention check) inside one pass.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large Language Models Have Intrinsic Self-Correction Ability
finding: Partly challenges Huang. With temperature 0 and neutral prompts, intrinsic correction no longer hurts and sometimes helps. Gains are small.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.92 -> 76.00 (CoT, order 1), 75.35 -> 74.77 (no CoT, order 1). GPT-4 CSQA 84.11 -> 84.60 with fair prompt but 66.34 and 72.56 with two biased prompt sets. HotpotQA GPT-3.5 31.00 -> 47.00 with fair prompt.
limits: Gains mostly inside noise on CSQA; significance claimed on pooled averages over six datasets.
agent_relevance: Wording matters: 'find the error' pushes models to change answers. Use neutral wording.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) Evaluating LLMs at Detecting Errors in LLM Responses (ReaLMistake, COLM)
finding: On realistic errors from GPT-4 and Llama 2 70B, 12 LLM detectors find errors at low recall; self-consistency does not help.
numbers: 900 instances with expert labels; expert F1 95.7. Strong models (GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus) have high precision, very low recall; higher LMSYS Elo means higher precision, lower recall. Wording change (detect errors vs evaluate validity) shifts recall by 16.9 +/- 20.3 points averaged over 12 LLMs.
limits: Zero-shot prompts; later reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Detection is the weak half. Do not take a model saying it looks fine as a stop sign.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Reasoning models are far better at locating the first bad step than non-reasoning models or process reward models.
numbers: 3,400 cases with expert first-error labels. F1: GPT-4o-0806 GSM8K 79.2, MATH 63.6, OlympiadBench 51.4, average 61.9; o1-mini 93.2, 88.9, 87.2, average 87.9. Open QwQ-32B-Preview competitive with GPT-4o. Trained PRMs generalize badly beyond GSM8K and MATH.
limits: Math only; critics judge others' solutions, not their own.
agent_relevance: Error-locating is improving with reasoning models, so G2 may soften later for such an agent; re-test.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST, NeurIPS D&B)
finding: A taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups from 1,600+ traces over 7 frameworks. Verification failures are a major group.
numbers: Annotator kappa 0.88; LLM judge kappa 0.77. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 frameworks. FM-3.1 premature termination 6.20%, FM-3.2 no or incomplete verification 8.20%, FM-3.3 incorrect verification 9.10%; FM-1.1 disobey task spec 11.8%; FM-1.5 not recognising completion 12.4%. Role-spec fix gave +9.4% success on ChatDev.
quote: Successful systems all work alike; each failing system has its own problems.
limits: Percentages are of annotated traces; modes can co-occur. Prompt fixes give modest gains.
agent_relevance: A checklist of slip types; make verification an explicit stage with checks beyond it compiles.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM Agents Fail and How They Can Learn from Failures (AgentDebug)
finding: Taxonomy of agent errors by module (memory, reflection, planning, action, system); an early root-cause error cascades. Targeted debug feedback lets agents recover.
numbers: AgentErrorBench from ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop. AgentDebug all-correct 24.3% vs 0.3% for strongest baseline; step accuracy 45.0% vs 28.0% (direct prompting 28.0%). GAIA step accuracy 58.0% vs 30.0%. Downstream task success up to 26% relative gain.
limits: The localiser is itself an LLM pipeline; benchmark built by the same authors.
agent_relevance: Locating the root-cause step and re-running from there beats unguided revision. Matches Tyen backtracking.

source: Shamsujjoha et al. (2025) Swiss Cheese Model for AI Safety: taxonomy and reference architecture for multi-layered guardrails of FM-based agents
finding: Reason's Swiss cheese idea carried into agent design: stacked guardrail layers across quality attributes, pipeline stages and artifacts so one failing layer does not pass a hazard.
numbers: Systematic review: 1,733 search hits, 174 papers screened, 32 primary studies after cross-check (as shown in the paper's method figure).
limits: A design taxonomy, not a measured effect; no failure-rate tests.
agent_relevance: Supports independent checks (code check, best-so-far, round cap) instead of one critic.

source: Cross-source synthesis of c01, c09, c11, c12, c16
finding: Across independent groups the pattern repeats: a hidden-answer or sound verifier gives big gains; a model judging itself gives none or loses; the loop's gain often equals extra sampling.
numbers: Verifier lift: Blocksworld 40% -> 88% (sound) vs 55% (LLM); graph coloring 16% -> about 40% (sound) vs 1% (LLM); code repair 33.3% -> 52.6% (human feedback).
limits: Compiled from the opened papers; not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: Keep G2 and S5 as written: located failing output, one named line, at most 2 rounds, keep best.
